what_its_for: Quinidine is used to treat certain irregular heartbeat problems (called arrhythmias). It helps your heart beat in a normal, steady rhythm. In some cases, it may also be used to treat a serious infection called malaria.
how_to_take: Take quinidine exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or break extended-release tablets. You can take quinidine with food or a full glass of milk to help prevent stomach upset. Try to take it at the same times every day to keep a steady level in your body. Do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor first.
dosing: Your dose will be set by your doctor based on your heart condition, weight, kidney function, and how well the medicine is working for you. Doses vary widely from person to person. The most important thing is to follow your doctor's specific instructions. Do not take more or less than prescribed, and do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is within 2 hours of when you were supposed to take it. If it has been more than 2 hours, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this can be dangerous for your heart.
storage: Store quinidine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep it in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines safely out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking grapefruit juice while taking quinidine, as it can increase the level of this medicine in your blood to unsafe levels. Avoid alcohol, as it can make side effects worse. Do not take antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium within 2 hours of your quinidine dose. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about all other medicines you take — including over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, and herbal supplements — because many medicines can interact with quinidine. Avoid driving or using heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, as it can sometimes cause dizziness.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: a fast, slow, or very irregular heartbeat; fainting or feeling like you might faint; severe dizziness or lightheadedness; ringing in your ears, hearing loss, or blurred vision; fever, chills, or unusual bruising or bleeding; chest pain or shortness of breath; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. These could be signs of a serious reaction that needs immediate attention.
when_it_works: Quinidine begins working within 1 to 3 hours of taking a dose. However, it may take several days of regular use before your heart rhythm is fully stabilized and you feel the full benefit. Keep taking it as directed even if you feel well, because stopping suddenly can be dangerous. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular checkups and possibly heart tests (like an EKG) and blood tests.
special_populations: Older adults may be more sensitive to the side effects of quinidine, especially dizziness and heart rhythm changes, and may need a lower dose. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, talk to your doctor before taking quinidine, as it may affect the baby. This medicine can pass into breast milk, so breastfeeding is generally not recommended while taking it — discuss this with your doctor. People with kidney or liver problems may need a lower dose and closer monitoring. Always tell all your healthcare providers that you take quinidine before any surgery, procedure, or new prescription.
